notes.text: Rest — A life of rest, and comfort, and safety, under the care of a good husband.
Threshing-floor — Which was in a place covered at the top, but open elsewhere, whither Ruth might easily come. And this work of winnowing corn was usually ended with a feast.
Raiment — Thy best raiment. Known - In so familiar a way, as thou mayest do hereafter.
Uncover his feet — Remove the clothes that were upon his feet; thereby to awaken him. Will tell thee - What course thou shalt take to obtain that marriage which belongs unto thee.

glossa.text: *The threshing-floor.* The synagogue of the Jews, where the barley of the law was stored: this Christ winnows, when, preaching the Gospel on the floor, he threshes out the counsels and the wills of each man toward himself; whence: *But Jesus did not trust himself unto them, for that he knew all men, and because he needed not that any should give testimony of man ((Joan. II))*.

*Let no man see thee.* Because the faith of the Church of the Gentiles did not appear before Christ had fulfilled the mystery of his incarnation, when, living bodily among men, he used food and drink, and at last, supping with his disciples, he shared with them the sacraments of his body and his blood. But when the mystery of the dispensation was fulfilled, the Church of Christ from the Gentiles came to the faith with confidence.

*Thou shalt uncover,* etc. What he says is: Acknowledge Christ as having suffered for thee, and come with a devout mind; shake off the covering of the letter of the Old Testament, in which the sacrament of Christ's incarnation is hidden; and when thou hast known that salvation was promised thee therein, flee humbly to his help, that thou mayest abide there at all times.

notes.text: Build — Assist and bless those that build it.
You — Builders, or watchmen. To sit - To use constant and unwearied diligence. So - By his blessing. Giveth - Freely, without that immoderate toiling, wherewith others pursue it.
Children — The chief of these blessings. Heritage - Only from God's blessing, even as an inheritance is not the fruit of a man's own labour, but the gift of God.

Youth — These he prefers before other children, because they live longest with their parents, and to their comfort and support, whereas children born in old age seldom come to maturity before their parents death.

Full — Who hath a numerous issue. Shall speak - They shall courageously plead their cause in courts of judicature, not fearing to be crushed by the might of their adversaries. The happiness of them that fear God, ver. 1-6. A song of degrees.

glossa.text: *A canticle of degrees of Solomon.* ((CASS.)) The eighth degree, etc., *as far as* and in himself, as the corner stone, he built up the Church of two walls, of the Jews and of the Gentiles. ((AUG.)) Here is added *of Solomon,* because it was he who built the temple, in a figure of Christ the peacemaker, who built the Church of two walls. Lest therefore thou shouldst understand that Solomon, he says, *Unless the Lord build.* In him is hope to be placed, but in no man: because even that Solomon fell who built the temple. ((CASS.)) First, he admonishes how they that ascend ought to bear themselves, namely that they learn that the building and the keeping are from none but God. And exaltation in the world to come is only after humiliation. Secondly, he tells what the inheritance is, and how it is gathered, there, *Behold the inheritance. Unless the Lord.* ((ID.)) As if he should say *dieeret*: now Jesus has come, he has brought back from captivity: now the city Jerusalem is being built; but let them that ascend learn that the building and the keeping are from none but God, and exaltation only after humiliation in the world to come; for although they are glad of the grace of the New Testament, yet in so great a gift no man ought to presume. *The house.* ((AUG.)) To this every man ascends who advances: from this every man falls who fails; by loving God thou ascendest, by loving the world thou fallest. For these are the songs of lovers, and of men burning with a certain holy desire. *They have laboured.* ((ID.)) All labour in this building who preach the word of God in the Church. *The city.* ((CASS.)) He passes from the house to the city, that presumption be made neither in individuals nor in a small gathering. And although house and city, according to the metaphor which is drawn from different things, are diverse: yet the Church is one, which both signify.

*Before the light.* ((AUG.)) If ye rise before the light rises; the light is Christ, after whom we must rise, not before; as he does who sets himself before him: wishing to be lofty here, where he was humble: as also the sons of Zebedee: but the resurrection, that is, the exaltation, follows the sitting, that is, the humiliation, as our light Christ rose lofty after death. *Ye shall have sat.* Sitting sometimes signifies the honour of judging, but here humiliation. *Ye that eat the bread of sorrow.* ((AUG.)) He eats the bread of sorrow who groans in this pilgrimage, that is, in the vale of weeping refreshes himself out of his affliction, saying: *My tears have been made my bread day and night ((Psal. XLI))* . *Sleep.* ((CASS.)) Temporal death, in which is a secure rest.

*Behold the inheritance.* ((ID.)) Secondly, what the inheritance is and how it is gathered. As if he should say, the beloved shall rise after sleep. *The fruit of the womb.* ((AUG.)) The womb of the Church, etc., *as far as* because he acquired all men through the obedience of his passion, *whence, ask of me, and I will give thee the Gentiles for thy inheritance ((Psal. II))*.

*As arrows.* ((ID.)) But whence so great an inheritance was made: because the Lord is mighty: when he shot forth the arrows, the apostles, mightily from the bow of holy Scripture, those that were shot forth reached unto the ends of the earth; and such are the *children of them that were shot forth,* as were they that were shot forth. *The children of them that were shot forth.* ((ID.)) The children of the apostles; to whom it was said, *Shake off the dust from your feet ((Matth. XVIII))*. But they so appear, etc., *as far as* who were sent by the hand of God unto the ends of the earth.

notes.text: For Christ did not enter into the holy place made with hands — He never went into the holy of holies at Jerusalem, the figure of the true tabernacle in heaven, chap. viii, 2. But into heaven itself, to appear in the presence of God for us - As our glorious high priest and powerful intercessor.

For then he must often have suffered from the foundation of the world — This supposes,

1. That by suffering once he atoned for all the sins which had been committed from the foundation of the world.

2. That he could not have atoned for them without suffering. At the consummation of the ages - The sacrifice of Christ divides the whole age or duration of the world into two parts, and extends its virtue backward and forward, from this middle point wherein they meet to abolish both the guilt and power of sin.
After this, the judgment — Of the great day. At the moment of death every man's final state is determined. But there is not a word in scripture of a particular judgment immediately after death.

Christ having once died to bear the sins — The punishment due to them. Of many - Even as many as are born into the world. Will appear the second time - When he comes to judgment. Without sin - Not as he did before, bearing on himself the sins of many, but to bestow everlasting salvation.

glossa.text: *Nor that he should offer himself often,* etc. He has proved that Christ by his own victim cleansed the heavenly things; now he proves that by better victims, that is, that his victim was worthier and more effectual than all others: because those, often repeated, were without consummation, this, offered once, brings back to our country.

*Otherwise,* etc. If, offered once, he did not suffice to exhaust the sins of all that believe in him, he must have suffered oftener from the beginning of the world; and that this might not be, he suffered once in the consummation of the ages. *In the consummation.* That is, in the last age, in which all those things are fulfilled which before were imperfect, and therefore there was no need that he should begin to suffer from the beginning of the world.

*And as.* The natural law shows this, which has been proved by the unfitting. *To die once.* It is not to be understood that Christ was offered by any necessity of his own sin, even once, but rather by will alone. But as a man once dead by necessity and by the law of nature dies no more, so also Christ, offered once by the same law, cannot die any more. *But after this.* After dying once, judgment remains, in which all shall receive according as they have deserved; but it does not remain that they should rise again, and die anew.

*He shall appear without sin.* So that then there shall not be a victim for sin, but justice in rewarding, or in condemning. But if there shall not be a victim even in the day of wrath, much less in other times. Or *without sin,* that is, without the likeness of the flesh of sin, but rather in glorious flesh.

notes.text: Beware of the scribes — There was an absolute necessity for these repeated cautions. For, considering their inveterate prejudices against Christ, it could never be supposed the common people would receive the Gospel till these incorrigible blasphemers of it were brought to just disgrace. Yet he delayed speaking in this manner till a little before his passion, as knowing what effect it would quickly produce. Nor is this any precedent for us: we are not invested with the same authority. Matt. xxiii, 5; Luke xx, 46.

He beheld how people cast money into the treasury — This treasury received the voluntary contributions of the worshippers who came up to the feast; which were given to buy wood for the altar, and other necessaries not provided for in any other way. Luke xxi, 1.

I say to you, that this poor widow hath cast in more than they all — See what judgement is cast on the most specious, outward actions by the Judge of all! And how acceptable to him is the smallest, which springs from self-denying love!

glossa.text: *Beware. ((BEDA.))* Note that he does not forbid those who are of this office, etc., *as far as* we be led astray by their pretence, or be inflamed by emulation to the same.

*Who devour the houses of widows.* As men who are to be patrons in the judgment, they do not hesitate to take money from the weak and from those troubled by the conscience of their sins: whereas it is the hand stretched out to give, and not closed to receive, that commends prayer to God: to whom that word is fitting: *Let his prayer be turned to sin.*

*The treasury. ((BEDA.))* Φυλάττειν in Greek, to keep in Latin. Gaza, in Persian, riches, Gazophylacium the place in which riches are kept, and the chest, namely, in which the offerings of the people were gathered for the uses of the temple. Whence in the book of Kings: *Joiada the high priest took one chest, and opened a hole in the top ((IV Reg. XII))*, etc., and the porches in which they were kept. Whence: *These words Jesus spoke in the treasury, teaching in the temple.*

*He beheld how.* As he said that those who seek after primacy and vainglory are to be avoided, and foretold a more grievous judgment to those who pray in pretence, so also he discerns those who offer with a just examination, that he may render to each according to the heart and the works, which he does also today in the Church.

*The rich. ((BEDA.))* The rich, the Jews puffed up over the justice of the law, etc., *as far as* they surpass all the works of the proud Jews.

*A poor widow. ((HIER.))* This poor little woman signifies me and such as me, who cast in what I can and desire what I cannot to expound to you. God desires not how much, but out of how much. *A farthing.* Reckoners call a farthing the fourth part of any thing, namely, of place, of time, of money. Perhaps therefore here it signifies the fourth part of a sicle, that is, five oboli.
*For all. ((BEDA.))* The Jew casts into the gifts out of that which abounds to him, etc., *as far as My God, his mercy shall prevent me ((Psal. LVIII))*.

notes.text: Zarephath — A city between Tyre and Sidon, called Sarepta by St. Luke iv, 26, and others. Zidon - To the jurisdiction of that city, which was inhabited by Gentiles. And God's providing for his prophet, first, by an unclean bird, and then by a Gentile, whom the Jews esteemed unclean, was a presage of the calling of the Gentiles, and rejection of the Jews. So Elijah was the first prophet of the Gentiles. Commanded - Appointed or provided, for that she had as yet no Revelation or command of God about it, appears from ver. 12.

She said — Therefore though she was a Gentile, yet she owned the God of Israel as the true God. Two sticks - A few sticks, that number being often used indefinitely for any small number. And die - For having no more provision, we must needs perish with hunger. For though the famine was chiefly in the land of Israel, yet the effects of it were in Tyre and Sidon, which were fed by the corn of that land. But what a poor supporter was this likely to be? who had no fuel, but what she gathered in the streets, and nothing to live upon herself, but an handful of meal and a little oil! To her Elijah is sent, that he might live upon providence, as much as he had done when the ravens fed him.

But make, &c. — This he requires as a trial of her faith, and obedience, which he knew God would plentifully reward; and so this would be a great example to encourage others to the practice of the same graces.
The barrel, &c. — The meal of the barrel So the cruse of oil for the oil of the cruse.

Many days — A long time, even above two years, before the following event about her son happened. And surely the increase of her faith to such a degree, as to enable her thus to deny herself and trust the promise, was as great a miracle in the kingdom of grace, as the increase of her oil in the kingdom of providence. Happy are they who can thus against hope believe and obey in hope.

Wasted not — See how the reward answered the service. She made one cake for the prophet and was repaid with many for herself and her son. What is laid out in charity is set out to the best interest, an upon the best securities.

glossa.text:
*A woman.* ((ISID.)) The widow whom the Lord feeds not with the bread of wheat but of the word is she who, her husband being dead, may marry whom she will, that is, having shaken off the yoke of servitude, takes upon her the sweet yoke of Christ, and the light burden.

((RAB.)) This widow signifies the Church of the Gentiles, etc., *as far as* it is said not to have failed.

((ID.)) The widow with whom Elias lodged, and whose meal and oil he blessed, is the synagogue of the Jews, which, widowed by the death of Moses, was nourishing a little son, that is, the carnal people of the Jews. He, at the coming in of Elias, that is, of our Saviour, was sick of the fever of unbelief, because he believed not in him, but despised him. Whence the mother Synagogue complains of the coming of the Saviour, as though he himself were the cause of the slaying of the people, saying: *What have I to do with thee,* etc. Hence it is that Caiphas saith: *It is expedient for you that one die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not ((Joan. XI))*.

((ID.)) As the prophet was not exasperated by the words of the widow, but rather had compassion, so our Redeemer is not exasperated by the malice of the Jews, but having compassion on his people took him from his mother's bosom, when he took him from the carnal observance of the law, and laid him upon his own bed, that is, showed him that he had life in his death, and stretched himself three times, while he instilled the faith of the Trinity.

notes.text: That day — As soon as ever he is dead. Thoughts - All his designs and endeavours either for himself or for others.

For ever — Both because he liveth forever to fulfil his promises, and because he is eternally faithful. The psalmist praises God for his care over the church, ver. 1-14. His government over all, ver. 15-18. His giving his word to Israel, ver. 19, 20.

glossa.text: *Alleluia.* ((CAS.)) This voice, as it were saving musics *musicas*; read *musica*, "a saving music", like a heavenly harmony, which delights not men only but angels also, setting forth the praise of God. And it is fitly prefixed to this psalm, where the just man exhorts his soul to the praise of God: because in adversities the soul is sometimes troubled, whether it will or no. Whence above: *Why art thou sad, O my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?* But that he may take away her disquiet, he suggests joy out of hope, if not out of the thing itself: *Hope in God,* etc. ((AUG.)) This soul, lifted up by hope, praises God here. ((CAS.)) First, he counsels himself, as it were all men, to praise, lest prayer be made among vain things; and as though acquiescing in the counsel, he affirms that he will praise there where he shall be able to praise fully. Secondly, he admonishes others not to hope in man, there: *Trust not.* Thirdly, he teaches that all hope is to be placed in the Almighty, there: *Blessed,* etc.

*Praise the Lord, O my soul.* But it is asked, by whom, and to whom, is this counsel given? If it be said that the flesh counsels the soul, this does not seem to be true, since counsel is wont to be given by the better and the worthier to the inferior: but the flesh is inferior to the soul. For the soul, although it be blamed because it is a sinner, is nevertheless called better by nature than the body that is praised in its own kind, because a spiritual nature excels the body, which it moves, rules, endows with sense, and apprehends: and being itself unbounded, it is near to the substance of God. So gold, blamed because it is foul, surpasses lead in purity, praise *laudatio*; read *laudato*, "that is praised": so too a bad man surpasses the best of horses. Counsel therefore is not given to the soul by the flesh, however greatly it be subdued and made peaceable: which nevertheless is dead because of sin. Nor yet does the mortal flesh counsel the immortal soul, because it is always beneath the soul; but the higher part of the soul, that is, the mind, which thinks upon the divine wisdom, cleaving to it and sighing after it, sees certain of its own parts troubled by the motions of the world, and hurried away to outward things by the desire of earthly goods: whence it calls it back to things inward and higher. Exhorting itself therefore according to its sensuality, it says: *Praise the Lord, O my soul.* For what pleases thee in this world? Divided among so many loves of the things of the ages, gather thyself to thy Author: here is peace and security for thee. Then the soul answers the mind, as one weighed down here and not able to leave off, as is meet. *I will praise in life.* Here in death I shall praise but thinly, because the body *is a load upon the soul, and the earthly habitation presseth down the sense that thinketh upon many things ((Sap. IX))*; here hope feeds us, life is in the world to come.

*In my life.* ((CAS.)) When I shall have cleaved to him perfectly, from whom to be parted, as now befalls, is death: but hope consoles, in which, living after a sort, it praises.

*As long as.* Not that at some time he shall not be, because he shall be for ever, and therefore truly long.

*Trust not,* etc. ((CAS.)) The second part. The counsel being given and confirmed, where he shall be able to praise fully, he admonishes them, as though set far off, and in the meantime while evils last (by which the soul is troubled), not to hope in man, but in God. ((AUG.)) Or, as one set in mind at the end of the world: he teaches them not to love things soon to end in place of things eternal; as if by my example also, *trust not,* etc. *In the children of men.* ((ID.)) In one son of man is salvation, and in him do ye hope. Not because he is a son of man, but because he is the Son of God. Not for that which he took from thee, but for that which he kept in himself.
*His spirit shall go forth,* etc. ((CAS.)) First he cleanses hearts by forbidding what is hurtful, that afterward he may aim at what is saving by admonishing to wholesome things.

*Blessed is he whose God is the God of Jacob.* ((CAS.)) The third part, where he teaches that the whole hope is to be placed in the Almighty, whom he describes from his works, that the Gentile world, so often confuted, may be still. ((AUG.)) Hurtful things being removed, he teaches what belongs to salvation, namely, in whom hope is to be placed. *His helper is his hope.* ((CAS.)) Of that Jacob himself he was so the helper, etc., *as far as* that is, of this true Jacob, as of that one.

*Who made heaven and earth.* ((ID.)) Because the worshippers of demons also have hope in their god, he determines in whom hope ought to be, that is, in Christ, and this he shows even to the end of the psalm, describing him through all things. *All things that are in them.* Lest thou think any other to be the creator, or that there exists a creator even of the smallest things.

*Who keepeth truth for ever.* ((CAS.)) Christ, who is the truth; every man is a liar. *He executeth judgment.* These two pertain to justice. Christ the judge avenges those who suffer for his name, and gives food to them that love him. *For them that suffer wrong.* ((AUG.)) Not every trouble is a wrong. What thou sufferest by right is not a wrong, as is that which the robber and other wicked men suffer. It is one thing therefore to suffer wrong, another to suffer punishment. For a man suffers punishment by right, but wrong is contrary to right.

*The Lord looseth them that are fettered.* ((CAS.)) This belongs to the abundance of his sweetness.

*The Lord lifteth up them that are cast down.* Whom the devil casts down, the Lord lifts up.

*He loveth the just.* ((CAS.)) Whom he sets in eternal blessedness.

*The fatherless and the widow he will receive.* *suseipiet* ((AUG.)) The whole Church of the Gentiles is come as a stranger to the fathers, a daughter not by flesh but by imitation.

*The fatherless* are all who are in pilgrimage, whose father is absent; and every faithful soul is a *widow* while the bridegroom is absent: whence they desire the more both the father and the bridegroom, and God protects them, not seen but desired.

*The Lord shall reign for ever.* ((CAS.)) This is of his magnificence.

He shall reign in us when our hearts shall be firm in him, which is not yet.

registers.label: Spare
lines: The teachers love the long robes and the best seats.
But God sees the widow at the treasury.
The rich gave out of their plenty;
she gave out of her poverty everything she had.
Two small coins, all she owned —
and the jar of meal was not spent.
Come, let us worship the God who lifts the poor.
We bring all that we are. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: At Zarephath a widow scraped the last handful of meal from the jar, certain it was her final meal — and the jar was not spent; day after day it did not run dry.
She gave out of her poverty all that she had.
At the temple another widow came to the treasury and dropped in two small coins, the least that anyone gave that day.
She gave out of her poverty all that she had.
The rich poured in out of their abundance; she put in everything she owned, her whole living.
She gave out of her poverty all that she had.
This is the God who keeps the jar full and lifts up the poor. Come, bring your whole life and worship.
She gave out of her poverty all that she had. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: The widow dropped in two small coins.
We bring all that we have.
She gave not from her plenty but from her need.
We bring all that we have.
At Zarephath the jar of meal was not spent.
We bring all that we have.
Come, let us worship the God who provides.
We bring all that we have. Amen.
